title: Card Walker becomes Disney's chairman
what: This year Card Walker replaced Donn Tatum as chairman of Walt Disney Productions. Disney's films are struggling at the box office; its parks earn most of the money.
why: The old guard in charge; their big bet on EPCOT and weak films set up the takeover fight of 1984. The month of the change is not confirmed; the remark on films and parks is a general characterisation from the history page, not a figure.

title: EPCOT Center opens in Florida
what: EPCOT Center opened at Walt Disney World on 1 October after an investment of more than one billion dollars. It opens in a year of recession.
why: A huge capital bet by the old management; the parks would later become the company's cash engine.

title: Tokyo Disneyland and the Disney Channel open
what: Tokyo Disneyland, the first Disney park outside the United States, opened on 15 April. On 23 April Disney launched the Disney Channel on American cable television.
why: Two of the most durable earners of the following decades, started under the management that was soon to be pushed out.
note: Add a note about Japan's soaring stock prices

title: Disney shares soar on takeover buying
what: Disney shares jumped in March amid heavy buying and talk of a takeover. The financier Saul Steinberg began buying the stock on 12 March, at about 50 dollars a share, attracted by Disney's land, film library and low share price compared with the value of its assets.
why: Explains the +34% month (market +1%). Steinberg's stake (12.2% by late April) was disclosed only later; whether his name was public by the end of March is not confirmed, so the news item should speak of takeover buying rather than name him.

title: Disney pays the raider to go away
what: Disney agreed to buy back Saul Steinberg's 4.2 million shares at 70.83 dollars each, 297.4 million dollars, plus 28 million for his expenses, giving him a profit of about 32 million dollars. He had offered to buy 37.9% of the company at 67.50 dollars a share. After the deal Disney's stock fell nearly 16 dollars to 49.50 in five trading days, and shareholders sued. Paying a raider to leave is called greenmail.
why: Explains the -24% month: the takeover premium vanished and Disney's debt doubled. It led directly to the change of management in September.

title: Disney picks France for Euro Disneyland
what: On 18 December Disney chose a site at Marne-la-Vallee, about 20 miles east of Paris, over Spain for a European Disneyland due to open in 1991. It could draw up to 10 million visitors a year and employ 10,000 people. French officials put the cost at 1.8 billion dollars, which Disney said 'sounds a little high'.
why: The start of the Euro Disney saga, which became the big disappointment of the early 1990s.

title: The Little Mermaid opens to strong reviews
what: Disney's animated musical The Little Mermaid opened on 17 November to strong reviews and ticket sales.
why: The first film of the 'Disney Renaissance' (to 1999) that filled the studio, parks and shops with new characters. The stock rose about 70% in 1989. Review 2026-10: title "revives Disney animation" was a hindsight judgement.

title: Disney president Frank Wells dies in a helicopter crash
what: Frank Wells, Disney's president and Michael Eisner's partner since 1984, died in a helicopter crash on 3 April. Since the two took over, Disney's stock market value has risen from about 2 billion to about 22 billion dollars. Euro Disney, which is losing money, has been negotiating with its banks over its debts since March.
why: The loss of the steadying partner; it was followed by Jeffrey Katzenberg's departure and the costly Ovitz episode.

title: Disney agrees to buy Capital Cities/ABC for 19 billion dollars
what: On 31 July Disney agreed to buy Capital Cities/ABC, owner of the ABC television network and 80% of the sports channel ESPN, for about 19 billion dollars in cash and Disney shares. Cap Cities shareholders can take one Disney share plus 65 dollars per share. Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, Cap Cities' largest shareholder, signed an agreement backing the deal.
why: The defining deal of the Eisner era: it turned a studio-and-parks company into a media group, and ESPN became its biggest profit earner for two decades.

title: Michael Ovitz leaves Disney after little more than a year
what: Michael Ovitz, the Hollywood agent Michael Eisner hired as Disney's president in 1995, is leaving the company after little more than a year.
why: Ovitz's costly exit became a symbol of Eisner's management troubles; the Pixar partnership led to the 2006 purchase. The severance and lawsuits are later history and were not checked. Review 2026-10: cut the Pixar sentence: the source dates the ten-year deal only to 1997, not to January.

title: The September attacks empty Disney's parks; the Bass family sells
what: After the attacks of 11 September air travel stopped and stock exchanges closed until 17 September. Tourism-dependent companies such as Disney were hit hard. On 20 September Disney said it had bought 50 million of its own shares from 'certain significant stockholders' at a discount, and Goldman Sachs bought another 85 million to resell; the Texas billionaire Sid Bass, a large Disney shareholder since 1984, was forced to sell his holdings to meet a margin call.
why: Explains the -27% month (market -8%). The worst stretch of the arc, -65% from 2000-04 to 2002-09; Disney had a net loss of 158 million dollars in 2001. The 8-K does not name the sellers; the Disney history page says Sid Bass was forced to sell in 2001 after a margin call. Whether his name was public by the end of September is not confirmed, so the news item may need to say 'large shareholders'.

title: Roy E. Disney quits and starts a campaign against Eisner
what: Roy E. Disney, Walt Disney's nephew, resigned as chairman of Disney's animation division and from the board, and fellow director Stanley Gold resigned with him. The two set up a 'Save Disney' campaign to push out chief executive Michael Eisner.
why: The revolt that led to the 2004 protest vote and Eisner's departure in 2005. The month is not confirmed by the sources read (the history page lists it under 2003).

title: Shareholders rebuke Eisner; Comcast bid rejected
what: At Disney's annual meeting 43% of the votes cast were withheld from Michael Eisner, and the board took the chairman's title away from him while keeping him as chief executive. The protest was led by Roy E. Disney and Stanley Gold, who quit the board last year. Earlier this year the cable company Comcast made an unsolicited offer for Disney worth about 54 billion dollars, which Disney's board rejected.
why: The low point of Eisner's later years; it set up his departure in 2005. The exact dates of the Comcast bid and its withdrawal were not confirmed; the beat is placed at the annual meeting.

title: Bob Iger chosen to succeed Eisner
what: Disney's board chose its president Bob Iger to succeed Michael Eisner as chief executive when Eisner retires at the end of September. Iger came to Disney with ABC in 1996.
why: Iger's 15 years at the top brought Pixar, Marvel, Lucasfilm and Fox, and the stock rose 371% against the S&P 500's 161%.

title: Disney buys Pixar for 7.4 billion dollars
what: On 24 January Disney agreed to buy Pixar, the computer animation studio behind Toy Story and Finding Nemo, for about 7.4 billion dollars in Disney shares. Pixar's chief executive Steve Jobs will join Disney's board.
why: The first of Iger's big brand purchases; it rebuilt Disney's animation.

title: Disney's profit holds up so far, but the recession looms
what: On 6 November Disney reported earnings per share of 2.28 dollars for its business year to September, 2.27 dollars excluding one-off items, up 18%. Quarterly earnings excluding those items were 43 cents, against 42 cents a year earlier. The shares have fallen with the market since September.
why: The calm before the earnings drop reported in February 2009; Disney shares fell 16% in October and 13% in November.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1001039/000119312508227930/dex991.htm (Disney earnings release of 6 November 2008, read 2026-10-03); data/out/dis.json price series

title: Recession cuts Disney's profit by a third
what: On 3 February Disney reported that profit fell 32% and revenue 8% in the last three months of 2008, with earnings of 45 cents a share against 63 cents a year earlier. 'We faced a challenging first quarter with many of our businesses impacted to various degrees by the economic downturn,' said chief executive Bob Iger.
why: Explains part of the -19% month (market -11%): the recession hit parks, advertising and DVD sales at once. The stock had lost about 30% in 2008.

title: Disney buys Marvel for 4 billion dollars
what: On 31 August Disney agreed to buy Marvel Entertainment, owner of Spider-Man, Iron Man and the X-Men, for about 4 billion dollars in cash and Disney shares; Marvel shareholders get 30 dollars a share in cash plus Disney stock.
why: The purchase behind the Marvel film series that dominated the box office in the 2010s.

title: Record year for Disney
what: On 10 November Disney reported record revenue and profit for its business year to October: earnings per share rose 24% to 2.52 dollars and net income 21% to 4.8 billion dollars. Chief executive Bob Iger called it a great year financially and strategically.
why: The Iger growth years: Pixar, Marvel and ESPN fees drove steady earnings gains, and the stock nearly tripled from the end of 2011 to the end of 2015.

title: Disney buys Lucasfilm and Star Wars
what: On 30 October Disney agreed to buy Lucasfilm, George Lucas's company and owner of Star Wars, for 4.05 billion dollars, about half in cash and half in Disney shares. Disney plans new Star Wars films.
why: Completes the trio of brand purchases (Pixar, Marvel, Lucasfilm) that drove the 2012-2015 run, when the stock roughly doubled.

title: Disney earnings jump 34%
what: On 5 February Disney reported record quarterly earnings, up 34% to 1.03 dollars a share, with double-digit growth in operating income in every business. Revenue rose 9% to 12.3 billion dollars.
why: Peak of the 2012-2015 run, when every business grew at once.

title: Cable subscribers start to leave ESPN
what: On 4 August Disney reported record quarterly profit, but said that subscriber numbers fell at some of its cable networks, offset at ESPN only by its new SEC Network. Investors fear that viewers cancelling cable packages will hurt ESPN, Disney's biggest profit earner. The whole market fell in August.
why: The first public sign of cord-cutting, the slow erosion of the cable business that shaped the next decade. The shares fell 15% in August, with the market down about 6%.

title: Disney agrees to buy most of 21st Century Fox
what: On 14 December Disney agreed to buy most of Rupert Murdoch's 21st Century Fox, including its film studio and cable channels such as FX and National Geographic, for 52.4 billion dollars in Disney shares. Comcast had also bid.
why: Disney's biggest deal ever; Comcast's counterbid forced the price up to 71 billion dollars before the deal closed on 20 March 2019. It brought content for streaming but also a lot of debt.

title: Disney+ will launch in November at 6.99 dollars
what: At an investor day on 11 April Disney announced that its streaming service Disney+ will launch in the United States on 12 November, for 6.99 dollars a month, with films and series from Disney, Pixar, Marvel, Star Wars and National Geographic. The Fox purchase was completed last month.
why: Explains the +23% month (market +4%): investors cheered a cheap, content-rich rival to Netflix.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney%2B (read 2026-10-03; citing Variety, 11 April 2019, 'Disney+ to Launch in November, Priced at $6.99 Monthly')

title: Ten million sign up for Disney+ on day one
what: Disney+ launched on 12 November in the United States, Canada and the Netherlands. A day later Disney said more than 10 million people had already signed up, despite log-in problems on the first day.
why: Confirmation of the streaming bet; the shares rose strongly in November.

title: Iger hands over to Chapek; then the pandemic closes the parks
what: On 25 February Bob Iger stepped down as chief executive and was succeeded by Bob Chapek, head of the parks division; Iger stays as executive chairman. In mid-March, as the coronavirus spread, Disney closed Disneyland, Walt Disney World and Disneyland Paris and suspended its cruises; its parks in Asia were already shut. Cinemas closed too.
why: The parks and films, Disney's biggest businesses, stopped at once; the shares fell 15% in February and 18% in March.

title: Disney+ passes 73 million subscribers in its first year
what: On 12 November Disney reported a loss for its business year because of the pandemic, but said Disney+ had more than 73 million paying subscribers after one year, 'far surpassing our expectations'.
why: Streaming plus a market-wide rally (the market rose 11% in November; see the market arc): the shares rose 22%.

title: Disney+ reaches 86.8 million; Disney raises its streaming targets
what: At an investor day on 10 December Disney said Disney+ had 86.8 million subscribers, a year after launch, and laid out plans for dozens of new Marvel and Star Wars series and films for streaming.
why: Explains the +22% month (market +4%) and the stock's all-time high in early 2021; investors priced Disney as a streaming company, which later reversed.

title: Chapek ousted; Iger returns as chief executive
what: On 8 November Disney reported weaker-than-expected results, with adjusted earnings of 30 cents a share against 37 a year earlier and large losses in streaming. On 20 November the board dismissed Bob Chapek and brought back Bob Iger as chief executive.
why: The stock lost about 44% in 2022 as streaming losses mounted; Iger's return marked the bottom area.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1744489/000174448922000192/dis-20221108.htm (Disney earnings release of 8 November 2022, read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Chapek (read 2026-10-03)

title: Activist Nelson Peltz targets Disney
what: The investment firm Trian has nominated its founder Nelson Peltz for election to Disney's board, against the board's wishes, and proposed changes to the company's bylaws. On 11 January Disney's board recommended shareholders reject him and named Nike's executive chairman Mark Parker as its next chairman.
why: Explains the +25% month (market +6%): pressure for cost cuts plus a broad rebound. Trian gave up the fight in February after Iger announced a restructuring (Disney filed further proxy material on 9 February; the details of that filing were not read).

title: Disney's streaming turns a profit
what: On 14 November Disney reported adjusted earnings up 39% for the quarter and 32% for the year. Its combined streaming businesses made an operating profit of 321 million dollars, Disney+ gained 4.4 million subscribers, and Pixar's Inside Out 2 and Marvel's Deadpool & Wolverine broke box-office records. Its parks had record revenue and profit for the year.
why: Proof that Iger's cost cuts and price rises were working; the shares rose 22% in November.

title: Disney beats forecasts and raises its outlook
what: On 7 May Disney reported quarterly revenue up 7% to 23.6 billion dollars and adjusted earnings up 20% to 1.45 dollars a share. Disney+ added 1.4 million subscribers instead of losing them, US parks profit rose 13%, and Disney raised its full-year earnings forecast to 5.75 dollars a share.
why: Explains the +24% month (market +6%), with the market up 6%.

title: Josh D'Amaro named Disney's next chief executive
what: On 3 February Disney's board unanimously chose Josh D'Amaro, head of the parks and experiences business, to succeed Bob Iger as chief executive from 18 March. Dana Walden becomes president and chief creative officer.
why: Where the arc stands: succession settled at last. The shares in 2026 are still below their 2021 peak.
